tips.title: Four terms, in order
tips.body: **Restriction enzymes** cut, leaving **sticky ends**; a **vector** carries the gene in; **ligase** joins it. The specification names exactly these four, and questions ask for the **stages including** them — so learn them as a sequence, not a list.

tips.title: Selective breeding selects; engineering inserts
tips.body: **Selective breeding** chooses which organisms **reproduce**, over **many generations**, using genes the species **already has**. **Genetic engineering** **inserts a gene directly**, in **one** step, and the gene can come from a **different species** entirely.

tips.title: Sticky ends are why the joining works
tips.body: A restriction enzyme cuts the two strands **unevenly**, leaving short **unpaired** sections. The gene and the vector cut with the **same** enzyme have **matching** sticky ends, so they pair up — which is what lets the gene go into the right place.

tips.title: Selective breeding reduces variation
tips.body: Choosing the same characteristic repeatedly narrows the **gene pool**, so the population becomes more **genetically similar** — and therefore more vulnerable to a **single disease**. This is the drawback questions most often want.

tips.title: Evaluate means both sides then a judgement
tips.body: The specification says **evaluate the benefits and risks**, including **practical and ethical** implications. A list of advantages is a partial answer — give both, name an ethical point, and reach a conclusion.

why.matters:
People have been changing other species for thousands of years by choosing which individuals breed. Every crop and every breed of dog is the result, and the method is natural selection with a human doing the selecting.

Genetic engineering does the same job by moving a **single gene**, often between species, in one generation. The aim is identical and the objections are not — which is why the specification asks you to weigh the benefits and risks of both.

examples.title: Why a chihuahua and a wolf are the same species
examples.body:
Every dog alive descends from wolves, and dogs and wolves can still interbreed to produce fertile offspring, which by the usual definition makes them one species. The differences were produced by people choosing which animals bred, over thousands of generations. That is **selective breeding**, and it is the same mechanism as natural selection with the environment replaced by a preference.

It also shows the cost. Choosing hard for one characteristic reduces variation in everything else, which is why pedigree breeds carry inherited disorders and why a crop bred for yield can be wiped out by a single disease. You get what you selected for, and you lose what you were not looking at.

nodes.text: A new breed, and less variation

visual.alt: A flow chart of selective breeding: from a varied population, choose the individuals with the characteristic wanted, breed only from those, and repeat over generations, ending with a new breed and less variation than before

examples.title: Why insulin is no longer taken from pigs
examples.body:
Insulin for people with type 1 diabetes used to be extracted from the pancreases of pigs and cattle — slow, expensive, and not quite human insulin.

The human **gene** for insulin is now inserted into bacteria, which then make the protein in a fermenter. It is genuinely human insulin, there is as much of it as is needed, and it avoids the religious and ethical objections some people have to using animal products. The usual objections to GM crops, such as genes spreading to wild plants, do not apply to bacteria kept in a sealed fermenter.

visual.alt: A flow chart of making insulin by genetic engineering: the human insulin gene is cut out and inserted into a bacterial plasmid, and the bacteria then make human insulin in a fermenter

examples.title: Two routes to the same crop
examples.body:
A wheat that resists a disease can be produced either way, and the argument is about the **route** rather than the result.

Selective breeding takes many generations, can only use genes that already exist in that species, and brings along whatever else is linked to them. Genetic engineering takes one generation, can take a gene from **any** species, and moves only the gene chosen. That precision is the case for it; the fact that it crosses between species, and that the long-term effects are less well known, is most of the case against.

visual.alt: A table comparing selective breeding, which uses genes from the same species over many generations and brings whatever is linked to them, with genetic engineering, which can move one gene from any species in a single generation

steps.title: Selective breeding
steps.body:
**Selective breeding is choosing which organisms reproduce, in order to develop desired characteristics.** Humans have done it for thousands of years, long before anyone knew what a gene was.

**The process** is the same whatever the organism:

1. **Choose** the individuals with the desired characteristic from the existing population.
2. **Breed** them together.
3. **Select** the offspring that best show the characteristic.
4. **Repeat** over **many generations**.

Each round increases the proportion of the population carrying the alleles for that characteristic, so the characteristic becomes steadily more pronounced.

**Its impact on food plants and domesticated animals**, which the specification asks for:

- **Crops** bred for higher **yield**, **disease resistance**, larger fruit or faster growth.
- **Cattle** bred for more **milk** or **meat**.
- **Sheep** bred for better **wool**.
- **Dogs and horses** bred for temperament, appearance or particular kinds of work.

Almost every food plant and domesticated animal alive today is the result of it.

**The central drawback: reduced variation.** Repeatedly breeding from the same small group of individuals **narrows the gene pool**, so the population becomes more **genetically similar**.

**Why that matters** is the same argument as for asexual reproduction. A genetically similar population has little resistance to a **new disease** — if one individual cannot resist it, few others can either, and a whole crop or herd can be lost. It also increases the chance of harmful **recessive alleles** pairing up, since closely related individuals are more likely to carry the same ones.

**There are ethical concerns too**, particularly where animals are bred for appearance to the point that their health suffers.

steps.title: Tissue culture
steps.body:
*(Biology only.)* **Tissue culture** is growing new organisms, or new tissue, from **small groups of cells** taken from a parent, in a **sterile nutrient medium**.

**The process for plants**: a small sample of tissue is taken from the parent plant, sterilised to remove microorganisms, and placed on a nutrient **growth medium** containing plant **hormones** which stimulate it to divide and develop into a whole plant.

**The offspring are clones** — genetically identical to the parent — because the cells divide by **mitosis**.

**Its advantages in plant breeding programmes**, which the specification asks for:

- **Many identical plants** can be produced from **one** parent, very **quickly**.
- A plant with a **desirable characteristic** can be multiplied **exactly**, without waiting for sexual reproduction and without the variation it introduces.
- Plants can be produced **all year round**, independently of the growing season.
- **Rare or endangered** plants can be propagated when few individuals remain.

**Its advantages in medical research:**

- Cells can be grown in **controlled conditions** to study how they behave.
- **Drugs can be tested** on cultured cells before any use in animals or people.
- Tissue can be grown for **transplant** or repair.
- Because the cells are **identical**, results are more **reliable** — differences between cells cannot explain away a result.

**The drawback is the same as everywhere else in this topic.** The plants produced are **genetically identical**, so there is **no variation**, and the whole population shares the same vulnerability to disease. It is also **expensive**, requires **sterile conditions**, and any infection spreads to the entire batch.

steps.title: The stages of genetic engineering
steps.body:
**Genetic engineering is a process which involves modifying the genome of an organism to introduce desirable characteristics.**

*(Higher tier only.)* The specification names four things the main stages involve: **restriction enzymes**, **ligase**, **sticky ends** and **vectors**.

visuals.problem: Describe the main stages of genetic engineering.

steps.text: **Identify and cut out the desired gene** using **restriction enzymes**
steps.note: these cut DNA at specific base sequences, so the gene can be released precisely

steps.text: The cut is **staggered**, leaving short unpaired sections called **sticky ends**
steps.note: the two strands are cut at different points, so a few bases are left overhanging

steps.text: **Cut the vector with the same restriction enzyme**, giving **matching sticky ends**
steps.note: this is the key step — the same enzyme cuts the same sequence, so the ends pair up

steps.text: The **vector** is usually a **plasmid** or a **virus** — something that can carry DNA into a cell
steps.note: a plasmid is a small circular loop of DNA found in bacteria

steps.text: The sticky ends of the gene and vector **pair together**, and **ligase** **joins them permanently**
steps.note: ligase seals the sugar-phosphate backbone; the sticky ends align it, ligase fixes it

steps.text: The **vector inserts the gene into the host cell**, which now expresses the new characteristic
steps.note: the host makes the protein the gene codes for, exactly as for its own genes

the staggered cut leaves short unpaired sections that join to matching ones

steps.title: GM crops, GM insulin, and feeding a growing population
steps.body:
*(Biology only.)* **Genetic engineering applied to crops** is what the specification asks you to evaluate, with a named example.

**The named example**: introducing **genes for insect resistance from *Bacillus thuringiensis*** into crop plants. The bacterium naturally produces a protein toxic to certain insects; moving the gene into the crop means the plant produces it itself.

**Advantages of GM crops:**

- **Higher yields**, because less of the crop is lost to pests — important for a growing population.
- **Less pesticide** needs to be sprayed, reducing cost and the effect on other species.
- Crops can be given **drought or disease resistance**, or improved **nutritional value**.
- The change is achieved in **one generation** rather than the 20 or more that selective breeding might take.

**Disadvantages and risks:**

- **Reduced variation**, since GM crops are genetically uniform.
- Genes might **spread to wild plants** through pollen, with unpredictable effects.
- Insects may **evolve resistance** to the toxin — by natural selection, exactly as bacteria do to antibiotics.
- Effects on **other organisms**, including insects that are not pests.
- **Long-term effects** on human health are not fully known, though no harm has been demonstrated.
- **Cost**, and concerns about farmers depending on companies that own the seed.

**Genetic engineering in medicine.** The specification asks about medicine as well as agriculture. The human gene for **insulin** is inserted into a bacterial **plasmid**, and the modified bacteria are grown in large **fermenters**, where they make **human insulin** for people with **type 1 diabetes**.

- **Benefits**: it is identical to human insulin, it can be made in large quantities, and it does not depend on the pancreases of pigs and cattle, which avoids the religious and ethical objections some people have to using animal products.
- **Risks and practical limits**: the bacteria must be grown in **sealed, sterile** fermenters, both to keep them in and to keep other microorganisms out, and the equipment is expensive.
- **Ethics**: some people object to modifying any organism, but the objections usually raised to GM crops, such as genes spreading to wild plants, do not apply to bacteria kept in a sealed fermenter.

*(Biology only.)* **Agricultural solutions to a growing population** more broadly, which the specification also asks for:

**Fertilisers** increase yield by supplying the minerals plants need. But excess washes into rivers, causing **eutrophication** — algae grow, block light, then decompose, and the oxygen used up kills fish.

**Biological control** uses a natural **predator** of the pest instead of a chemical. It avoids pesticide residues and the pest is less likely to become resistant — but it works **slowly**, rarely removes the pest entirely, and the introduced species may itself become a problem.

steps.title: Going deeper
steps.body:
*(Higher tier only.)* **Name all four terms, in order.** **Restriction enzymes** cut, leaving **sticky ends**; **ligase** joins the gene into the **vector**; the vector carries it into the host cell. Questions ask for the stages **including** these, so missing one costs a mark directly.

*(Higher tier only.)* **Explain what sticky ends are for.** The restriction enzyme cuts the two strands **unevenly**, leaving short **unpaired** sections. Cutting the **gene and the vector with the same enzyme** gives **matching** ends, so they pair together correctly. Naming sticky ends without saying why they matter is half an answer.

**Distinguish the two techniques by mechanism, not just speed.** **Selective breeding** works with alleles the species **already has**, by choosing who **reproduces**, over **many generations**. **Genetic engineering** **inserts a gene directly**, in essentially **one step**, and the gene may come from a **completely different species** — which selective breeding can never do.

**Give reduced variation as the central genetic risk**, for selective breeding, tissue culture and GM crops alike. In a genetically uniform population, if one individual cannot resist a **new disease**, none of the others can either, so a single pathogen can destroy all of it. It is the same argument as for asexual reproduction.

*(Biology only.)* **Use the specification's named example.** **Insect resistance from *Bacillus thuringiensis*** introduced into crop plants. A named example is worth more than a general claim about GM crops.

*(Biology only.)* **Apply natural selection to GM crops.** If a crop produces an insect toxin continuously, any insect with a **chance mutation** conferring resistance survives and reproduces — so resistance **spreads**, exactly as antibiotic resistance does in bacteria. Making that connection shows the topics joining up.

*(Biology only.)* **Explain eutrophication as a chain**: excess fertiliser washes into rivers → **algae grow** → light is **blocked** → plants die and **decompose** → decomposers use up the **oxygen** → **fish die**. Each arrow is a link, and the chain is what earns the marks.

**Evaluate properly.** The command is to **evaluate the benefits and risks**, including **practical and ethical implications**. So: benefits, risks, an **ethical** point — such as animal welfare in selective breeding, or farmers' dependence on seed companies — and then a **judgement** that says what it depends on.

steps.title: Summary
steps.body:
- **Selective breeding**: choose, breed, select, **repeat over many generations**.
- It uses alleles the species **already has**.
- Impacts: crop **yield** and disease resistance; **milk, meat, wool**, temperament.
- Its main drawback is **reduced variation**, so vulnerability to a **single disease**.
- Harmful **recessive alleles** are also more likely to pair up.
- **Tissue culture** grows organisms from small groups of cells on a nutrient medium.
- The offspring are **clones**, because the cells divide by **mitosis**.
- It allows **many identical plants quickly**, **all year round**, and helps **rare** species.
- In medicine it allows **controlled study**, **drug testing** and **reliable results**.
- **Genetic engineering** modifies the **genome** to introduce **desirable characteristics**.
- **Restriction enzymes** cut the gene out, leaving **sticky ends**.
- The **vector** — often a **plasmid** — carries the gene in; **ligase** joins it.
- Cutting gene and vector with the **same enzyme** gives **matching** sticky ends.
- Named example: **insect resistance from *Bacillus thuringiensis*** in crop plants.
- In medicine, **GM bacteria make human insulin** in sealed fermenters.
- **Fertilisers** raise yield but can cause **eutrophication**; **biological control** avoids residues but is slow.

questions.prompt: Describe the main stages of genetic engineering, and explain how it differs from selective breeding.
questions.solution:
**Genetic engineering is a process which involves modifying the genome of an organism to introduce desirable characteristics.** The main stages involve four things the specification names.

**Cutting out the gene.** **Restriction enzymes** cut DNA at **specific base sequences**, which allows the desired gene to be released precisely rather than at random.

**Sticky ends.** The restriction enzyme cuts the two DNA strands at **slightly different points**, so the cut is **staggered** and leaves short **unpaired sections** of bases overhanging. These are the **sticky ends**.

**Cutting the vector with the same enzyme.** This is the step that makes the whole process work. Because a restriction enzyme always cuts at the **same sequence**, using the **same enzyme** on the vector leaves it with **complementary** sticky ends. The gene's overhang and the vector's overhang then **pair together** by base pairing, holding the gene in exactly the right place.

**Joining with ligase.** The sticky ends align the pieces, but they are held only by weak hydrogen bonds. **Ligase** then **joins them permanently**, sealing the sugar-phosphate backbone so the gene becomes a genuine part of the vector's DNA.

**Inserting into the host.** The **vector** — usually a **plasmid**, a small circular loop of DNA found in bacteria, or sometimes a **virus** — carries the gene into the **host cell**. The host then expresses the gene, producing the protein it codes for and so showing the new characteristic.

**How this differs from selective breeding.**

**Selective breeding** works entirely through **reproduction**. Individuals with a desired characteristic are chosen and bred together, the best offspring are selected, and the process is **repeated over many generations** — perhaps twenty or more. Each round increases the proportion of the population carrying the relevant alleles.

The crucial limitation is that it can only work with **alleles the species already has**. A characteristic can be made more common, or more pronounced, but nothing genuinely new can be introduced.

**Genetic engineering** inserts a gene **directly**, in essentially **one step**, and produces the modified organism **immediately** rather than after decades of breeding.

More importantly, the gene can come from a **completely different species**. The specification's example is introducing genes for **insect resistance from *Bacillus thuringiensis*** — a **bacterium** — into **crop plants**. No amount of selective breeding could ever achieve that, because the plants do not have the gene to begin with.

So the difference is not simply one of speed. Selective breeding **rearranges what exists**; genetic engineering **adds something that did not**.

The crucial limitation is that it can only work with **alleles the species already has**. A characteristic can be made more common, or more pronounced, but nothing genuinely new can be introduced.

**Genetic engineering** inserts a gene **directly**, in essentially **one step**, and produces the modified organism **immediately** rather than after decades of breeding.

More importantly, the gene can come from a **completely different species**. The specification's example is introducing genes for **insect resistance from *Bacillus thuringiensis*** — a **bacterium** — into **crop plants**. No amount of selective breeding could ever achieve that, because the plants do not have the gene to begin with.

So the difference is not simply one of speed. Selective breeding **rearranges what exists**; genetic engineering **adds something that did not**.

questions.prompt: Evaluate the benefits and risks of genetically modifying crops to feed a growing human population, including practical and ethical implications.
questions.solution:
**The benefits.** The clearest is **higher yield**. Crops modified for **insect resistance** lose less of the harvest to pests — the specification's named example is introducing genes for insect resistance from ***Bacillus thuringiensis*** into crop plants, so that the plant itself produces a protein toxic to certain insects. For a growing human population, producing more food from the same land is a substantial gain.

It also means **less pesticide** needs to be sprayed. That reduces cost for the farmer, reduces residues on the food, and reduces harm to insects that were never the target — so a GM crop can be better for the surrounding environment than a heavily sprayed conventional one.

Crops can also be engineered for **drought resistance**, **disease resistance** or improved **nutritional value**, which matters where a population depends heavily on a single staple crop.

And it is **fast**. Selective breeding might take **twenty generations or more** to shift a characteristic, and can only use alleles the species already has. Genetic engineering achieves the change in **one step**, and can bring in a gene from **another species** entirely.

**The risks.** **Genes may spread to wild plants** through pollen, producing wild relatives with herbicide or insect resistance, with effects that are hard to predict and impossible to recall once they have happened.

**Insects may evolve resistance** to the toxin. This follows directly from natural selection: a **chance mutation** gives some insects resistance, the toxin **kills the rest**, and the survivors **reproduce and pass on the allele**. A crop producing the toxin continuously is an unusually strong and unrelenting selection pressure, so resistance can spread quickly — exactly as antibiotic resistance does in bacteria. The benefit may therefore be **temporary**.

**Reduced variation** is a risk GM crops share with selective breeding and tissue culture. In a genetically uniform crop, if one plant **cannot resist a new disease**, none of the others can either, so a single pathogen could destroy all of it.

There may be effects on **other organisms**, including beneficial insects, and **long-term effects on human health** are not fully established — though it should be said that no harm has been demonstrated despite extensive use.

**Ethical implications** matter here too. Seeds are often owned by **large companies**, so farmers may become **dependent** on buying them each year rather than saving their own — a particular concern for farmers in poorer countries, who are among those the technology is supposed to help. Some people also object to moving genes between species on principle, and there are questions about whether consumers are given a genuine **choice** through labelling.

**Judgement.** On balance the benefits of GM crops are real and the risks are **manageable rather than prohibitive**, so I would support their use — but the decision depends on **how they are used and by whom**.

The technology addresses a genuine problem: feeding a growing population without clearing more land. The insect-resistance risk is serious but is a reason for **managing** the technology carefully — for instance by planting unmodified refuges so that resistance spreads more slowly — rather than for abandoning it.

The concerns I find hardest to dismiss are not biological but **ethical**: the concentration of seed ownership, and farmers' dependence on companies. Those are not solved by better science, and they determine whether the benefits reach the people who most need them.

It is also worth noting that GM is **not the only option**. **Fertilisers** raise yields but risk **eutrophication** — excess minerals wash into rivers, algae grow and block the light, plants die and decompose, and decomposers use up the **oxygen**, killing fish. **Biological control** avoids residues and resistance but works slowly and may introduce a new problem species. Every approach to feeding more people carries a cost, which is why the question is which risks are most acceptable rather than whether any exist.

names Bacillus thuringiensis insect resistance
gene spread and reduced variation
insect resistance by natural selection, and an ethical point
weighs the two sides
reaches a judgement naming what it depends on

questions.prompt: Insulin for people with type 1 diabetes used to be extracted from the pancreases of pigs and cattle. It is now made by bacteria that have been given the human insulin gene. Which is a benefit of the new method?
questions.solution: The bacteria make **human insulin**, identical to the person's own, and they can be grown in **large quantities**, without depending on animal pancreases. The bacteria do not change the patient's genes, so they cannot stop diabetes being inherited or cure it; insulin **treats** type 1 diabetes. The fermenters must still be kept **sterile**.

One dose of it cures type 1 diabetes for good

questions.prompt:
The table gives example figures for the yield of a wheat crop grown with different amounts of fertiliser.

| Fertiliser (kg per hectare) | Yield (tonnes per hectare) |
| --- | --- |
| 0 | 4.0 |
| 50 | 5.6 |
| 100 | 6.6 |
| 150 | 7.0 |
| 200 | 7.1 |

What does the data suggest about adding more than 150 kg of fertiliser per hectare?
questions.solution: Each extra 50 kg adds less yield: **1.6**, then **1.0**, then **0.4**, then only **0.1** tonnes per hectare. Above 150 kg per hectare the extra fertiliser gives **little extra yield**, while more of it is left in the soil, where it can be washed into rivers and cause **eutrophication**. The yield still rises a little, so it neither falls, nor doubles, nor stays unchanged.

options: It doubles the yield for every extra 50 kg
It adds little yield, and more is left to wash away
It lowers the yield, because the extra crop is poisoned

questions.prompt: Which of these describes genetic engineering?
questions.solution: **Modifying the genome of an organism to introduce desirable characteristics.** The genome is the entire DNA of an organism, and genetic engineering changes it directly, usually by inserting a gene, which may come from a different species. Choosing which organisms breed over many generations is **selective breeding**, which works only with alleles the species already has. Growing new plants from small groups of cells on a nutrient medium is **tissue culture**, which makes clones. Adding fertiliser supplies minerals to crops and does not change their DNA at all.

markScheme.description: modifying the genome of an organism to introduce desirable characteristics

options: Choosing which organisms breed together over many generations of a crop
Growing whole new plants from small groups of cells on a nutrient medium
Adding nitrate fertiliser to the soil so that the crops grow larger and faster
Modifying the genome of an organism to introduce desirable characteristics

questions.prompt: In medical research, a new drug is tested on cultures of human cells grown from a single sample of tissue, so all the cells are genetically identical. Why is it an advantage that the cells are genetically identical?
questions.solution: **A difference in how the cells respond can be put down to the drug, not their genes.** Because the cultured cells are clones, genetic differences between them cannot explain a result, so the results are more reliable, and the cells can be grown in controlled conditions. This is one of the advantages of tissue culture in medical research. Identical cells can still be damaged by a drug, which is exactly what the tests are looking for. Testing on cultured cells comes before testing in animals and people; it does not replace clinical trials. And cultured cells divide by **mitosis**, which is why they are identical, not by meiosis.

markScheme.description: any difference in response is due to the drug, not to genetic differences between the cells

options: Genetically identical cells cannot be damaged by a drug, so any dose of it is safe
Results from identical cells mean that the drug never has to be tested on people
A difference in how the cells respond can be put down to the drug, not their genes
Identical cells divide by meiosis, so they show the full range of human variation

questions.prompt: Farmers who grow a crop containing the gene for the Bt toxin from Bacillus thuringiensis are often advised to plant an area of the same crop without the gene nearby. Insects feeding in that area are not exposed to the toxin. How does this slow the spread of resistance to the toxin among the insects?
questions.skill: slowing resistance to a GM crop
questions.solution: **Non-resistant insects survive there and breed, so the resistance allele spreads more slowly.** Resistance to the Bt toxin spreads by natural selection. In a field of Bt crop alone, any insect with a chance mutation giving resistance survives while the others die, so only resistant insects breed, and the allele quickly becomes common. In the area without the gene, non-resistant insects survive and reproduce as normal, so they remain a large part of the population and breed with any resistant survivors, and the proportion carrying resistance rises far more slowly. The toxin is made inside the Bt plants, and insects feeding in the other area are not exposed to it. Insects in any area can mutate, and plants do not break down the Bt toxin made by their neighbours.

markScheme.description: non-resistant insects survive and breed there, so the resistance allele becomes common more slowly

options: The Bt toxin spreads out from the crop into the other area and kills the insects feeding there
Non-resistant insects survive there and breed, so the resistance allele spreads more slowly
Insects feeding on plants without the gene cannot mutate, so no resistance allele ever arises
The plants without the gene take up the Bt toxin from the soil and break it down harmlessly

questions.prompt: Human insulin is made by genetically modified bacteria grown in sealed fermenters, while Bt maize is grown in open fields. Why is the risk of the inserted gene spreading to wild organisms usually considered lower for the insulin-making bacteria?
questions.skill: weighing risks in medicine and agriculture
questions.solution: **The bacteria are kept sealed in, so the gene has little chance of reaching wild organisms.** A GM crop grows in the open, so its pollen can carry the inserted gene to other crops or, where they grow, to wild relatives, with unpredictable effects. The insulin-making bacteria are grown in **sealed, sterile** fermenters, both to keep them in and to keep other microorganisms out, so that route is closed, though an accidental release or careless disposal of waste could still let some escape. Bacteria can take up new genes, which is how the human insulin gene gets into them on a plasmid in the first place. Insulin is a protein, a hormone made by the pancreas. And the bacteria are alive throughout: they are the ones making the insulin.

markScheme.description: the bacteria are contained in sealed fermenters, so the gene has little chance of reaching wild organisms

options: Bacteria cannot take up new genes, so the insulin gene stays where it was inserted
Insulin is not a protein, so its gene cannot be passed on to any other living cell
The bacteria are kept sealed in, so the gene has little chance of reaching wild organisms
The bacteria are all killed before the gene is inserted, so no GM organism exists

questions.prompt: In genetic engineering, a vector carries the gene into the host cell. Name the type of vector that is a small ring of DNA found in bacteria.
questions.solution: **A plasmid.** Plasmids are small rings of DNA found in bacteria, separate from the main chromosomal DNA. The same restriction enzyme cuts the plasmid and the gene, leaving matching sticky ends; ligase joins the gene into the plasmid; and the plasmid carries the gene into the host cell, for example a bacterium that will then make human insulin.

questions.prompt: A dairy farmer starts a selective breeding programme with a herd whose mean milk yield is 6400 litres per cow per year. After five generations of breeding from the highest-yielding cows, a sample of five cows from the herd give yields of 8100, 7900, 8300, 7700 and 8000 litres per year. Using the mean yield of these five cows, calculate the mean increase in milk yield per generation, in litres per year.
questions.skill: the yield gain from a breeding programme
questions.solution:
Mean of the sample: $8100 + 7900 + 8300 + 7700 + 8000 = 40\,000$, and $40\,000 \div 5 = 8000$ litres per year.

Total increase: $8000 - 6400 = 1600$ litres per year.

Increase per generation: $1600 \div 5 = 320$ litres per year.

Check: $6400 + 5 \times 320 = 8000$. Each round of choosing the highest-yielding cows to breed from makes the alleles for high yield more common in the herd, which is why the mean rises generation after generation.

questions.prompt: A farmer grows maize on 50 hectares. Without any pest damage, the crop would yield 8.0 tonnes per hectare. Ordinary maize loses 15% of this yield to caterpillars, while Bt maize, which contains a gene for insect resistance from Bacillus thuringiensis, loses only 2%. Calculate how many more tonnes of maize the farmer would harvest from the whole 50 hectares by growing Bt maize instead of ordinary maize.
questions.skill: the yield benefit of an insect-resistant crop
questions.solution:
Harvest per hectare: ordinary maize keeps 85%, so $8.0 \times 0.85 = 6.8$ tonnes; Bt maize keeps 98%, so $8.0 \times 0.98 = 7.84$ tonnes.

Difference per hectare: $7.84 - 6.8 = 1.04$ tonnes. (Or directly: the Bt crop loses $15 - 2 = 13$ percentage points less, and 13% of 8.0 is 1.04 tonnes.)

Whole farm: $1.04 \times 50 = 52$ tonnes.

Check: ordinary maize gives $6.8 \times 50 = 340$ tonnes, Bt maize $7.84 \times 50 = 392$ tonnes, and $392 - 340 = 52$. This is the main advantage claimed for Bt crops: less of the yield is lost to insect pests, and less insecticide needs to be sprayed.

markScheme.description: finds the harvest per hectare of each (6.8 t and 7.84 t), or 13% of 8.0 = 1.04 t; any valid route
multiplies the difference per hectare by 50, or finds each total for 50 hectares and subtracts
52 tonnes

questions.prompt: A plant breeder has produced one strawberry plant with unusually large fruit that also resists a fungal disease. Describe how tissue culture could be used to produce thousands of plants with exactly the same characteristics, and explain why plants grown from its seeds would not all have them.
questions.solution: Small pieces of tissue, a few cells each, are cut from the parent plant and **sterilised** to remove microorganisms. They are placed on a sterile **nutrient growth medium** containing plant **hormones**, where the cells divide by **mitosis** and develop into small plants, which can be divided again to give thousands. Every one is a **clone**, genetically identical to the parent, so all have its large fruit and disease resistance. Seeds come from **sexual reproduction**: meiosis and fertilisation produce new combinations of alleles, and the pollen may come from a different plant, so the seedlings vary and many would lack one or both characteristics.

grown on a sterile nutrient medium with plant hormones; cells divide by mitosis into clones of the parent
seeds come from sexual reproduction, which produces new combinations of alleles, so seedlings vary

criteria.text: Describes cutting small pieces of tissue from the parent plant and sterilising them to remove microorganisms
Describes growing them on a sterile nutrient medium containing plant hormones, where the cells divide by mitosis into plants that are clones of the parent
Explains that seeds come from sexual reproduction, where meiosis and fertilisation produce new combinations of alleles, so the seedlings vary and many would lack the characteristics

questions.modelAnswer: To use tissue culture, the breeder cuts many small pieces of tissue, each only a few cells, from the parent plant, for example from the growing tips of its shoots. The pieces are sterilised to kill any microorganisms on them, because bacteria or fungi would grow on the nutrient medium and spread through the whole batch. Each piece is then placed on a sterile nutrient growth medium containing plant hormones, which stimulate the cells to divide and to develop into a small plant with shoots and roots. The cells divide by mitosis, so every new plant is a clone, genetically identical to the parent, with the same large fruit and the same resistance to the fungus. The small plants can be divided and cultured again, so thousands can be produced quickly and at any time of year, before being planted out. Seeds would not do this, because they are the product of sexual reproduction. Meiosis makes gametes with different combinations of the parent's alleles, and at fertilisation these combine with the alleles in the pollen, which may have come from another plant. Each seedling therefore has a new combination of alleles, so the offspring vary, and many would not have both of the parent's useful characteristics.

questions.prompt: Chickens reared for meat have been selectively bred to grow much faster than their ancestors, reaching slaughter weight in about six weeks. Some of these birds now grow so quickly that their legs struggle to support their weight. Explain how selective breeding produced the fast growth, and give one practical and one ethical implication of breeding chickens in this way.
questions.skill: implications of selective breeding in animals
questions.solution: Breeders chose the **fastest-growing** birds and bred them together, then chose the fastest-growing of their offspring, and **repeated** this over **many generations**, so the alleles for fast growth became more and more common in the flock. **Practical** (any valid one): more meat is produced quickly and cheaply, helping to feed a growing population; or the flock has **reduced variation**, so a new disease that one bird cannot resist could spread through all of them. **Ethical** (any valid one): the birds' welfare suffers, since legs that struggle to support their weight cause pain and difficulty moving, which raises the question of whether cheaper meat justifies breeding animals that suffer.

markScheme.description: the fastest-growing birds were bred together, the fastest offspring chosen, and this repeated over many generations
any valid practical implication (e.g. more meat produced cheaply; reduced variation, so a new disease could affect the whole flock)
any valid ethical implication (e.g. the birds' welfare suffers, with pain from legs that struggle to support them)

criteria.text: Explains that breeders chose the fastest-growing birds to breed together, selected the fastest-growing offspring, and repeated this over many generations, so the alleles for fast growth became more common
Gives any valid practical implication (e.g. more meat produced more quickly and cheaply for a growing population; or reduced variation, so a single new disease could affect the whole flock)
Gives any valid ethical implication (e.g. the birds' welfare suffers, because legs that struggle to support their weight cause pain, which raises the question of whether cheaper food justifies it)

questions.modelAnswer: Selective breeding works with the variation that already exists in a population. In each generation, the breeders chose the birds that grew fastest and bred them together. From their offspring they again chose the fastest-growing birds to breed, and they repeated this over many generations. Each round increased the proportion of the flock carrying the alleles for rapid growth, so the characteristic became more and more pronounced, until the birds reached slaughter weight in about six weeks rather than several months. One practical implication is that farmers can produce a large amount of meat quickly and cheaply, which helps to feed a growing human population. Another is that breeding repeatedly from a small group of similar birds reduces the variation in the flock: if a new disease appears and one bird cannot resist it, few of the others will be able to either, so a whole flock could be lost. The ethical implication is animal welfare. Birds whose legs struggle to support their weight are likely to be in pain and to have difficulty moving, so people disagree about whether cheaper meat justifies breeding animals in a way that causes them to suffer.

questions.prompt: A farmer needs to increase the yield of a lettuce crop to meet the demand from a growing population. The soil is short of nitrates, and the crop is attacked by aphids, small insects that feed on the plants. A river runs along one edge of the field. Explain the advantages and disadvantages of using fertilisers and biological control on this farm.
questions.solution: **Fertiliser** supplies the nitrates the lettuces lack; plants use nitrates to make **proteins** for growth, so the yield rises. But excess fertiliser that the crop does not take up can **wash into the river**, causing **eutrophication**: algae grow rapidly and **block the light**, water plants die, and **decomposers** breaking down the dead material **use up the oxygen**, so fish die. Fertiliser the crop does not use is also money wasted. **Biological control** means releasing a natural **predator** of the aphids, such as ladybirds. It reduces the damage without a chemical pesticide, so no residues are left on the lettuces, other species are not poisoned, and the aphids are less likely to become resistant. But it works **slowly** and rarely removes the pest completely, since the predators decline as the aphids become scarce, and an introduced predator may **become a problem itself**, for example by feeding on other, harmless insects.

markScheme.description: Level 1 (1 to 2 marks): gives an isolated advantage or disadvantage of one solution, such as that fertiliser increases yield or that biological control uses a predator, with little explanation

Level 2 (3 to 4 marks): explains an advantage and a disadvantage of one solution in some detail, such as the eutrophication chain, or gives advantages and disadvantages of both with only partial explanation

Level 3 (5 to 6 marks): explains why fertiliser raises the yield and the full eutrophication chain from fertiliser washing into the river; and explains at least one advantage of biological control (e.g. no chemical residues, other species unharmed, resistance less likely) and at least one disadvantage (e.g. slow, rarely removes the pest completely, the predator may become a problem itself)

criteria.text: Explains that fertiliser supplies minerals such as nitrates, which plants use to make proteins for growth, so the yield increases
Explains that excess fertiliser can wash into the river, where algae grow rapidly and block the light, so water plants die
Explains that decomposers breaking down the dead material use up the oxygen in the water, so fish and other animals die (eutrophication)
Explains that biological control uses a natural predator of the aphids, such as ladybirds, so pest damage falls and the yield rises
Gives a valid advantage of biological control over pesticides (e.g. no residues on the lettuces, other species not poisoned, or the aphids less likely to become resistant)
Gives a valid disadvantage of biological control (e.g. it works slowly and rarely removes the pest completely, or the introduced predator may become a problem itself)

questions.modelAnswer:
**Fertilisers.** The soil is short of nitrates, and plants need nitrates to make amino acids and **proteins** for growth. Adding fertiliser replaces them, so the lettuces grow larger and the **yield increases**, which is exactly what the farmer needs. The disadvantage comes from the river. Fertiliser that the crop does not take up can be washed by rain into the water, causing **eutrophication**. The extra minerals make **algae grow rapidly** on the surface and **block the light**, so the plants below cannot photosynthesise and die. **Decomposers** break down the dead plants and algae and, as they respire, **use up the oxygen** in the water, so fish and other animals die. Any fertiliser washed away is also money spent for nothing, so it pays to add only what the crop can use.

**Biological control.** Instead of spraying a pesticide, the farmer can release a natural **predator** of the aphids, such as ladybirds. The predators eat the aphids and reduce the damage, so the yield rises. Because no chemical is used, **no residues** are left on lettuces that people will eat raw, other insects are not poisoned, and the aphids are **less likely to become resistant** than they would be to a pesticide. But biological control works **slowly**, and it **rarely removes the pest completely**: as the aphids become scarce, the predators run short of food and their numbers fall too, so some damage continues. The introduced predator may also **become a problem itself**, for example by feeding on harmless or useful insects.

Used carefully, with fertiliser matched to what the crop needs, the two together can raise the yield while limiting the harm to the river.

examTechnique.body:
Name **all four** terms in order: **restriction enzymes** cut, leaving **sticky ends**; a **vector** carries; **ligase** joins. Explain that the **same enzyme** on gene and vector gives **matching** ends.

Separate the techniques by **mechanism**: selective breeding uses **existing alleles** over many generations; engineering **inserts a gene**, possibly from another species. **Evaluate** means both sides plus a judgement.
examinerErrors: Giving only two or three of the four named terms.
Naming sticky ends without explaining what they do.
Distinguishing the techniques only by how long they take.
Omitting reduced variation as a risk.
Giving no named example for GM crops.
Describing eutrophication without the chain of consequences.
Listing advantages only when asked to evaluate.
Forgetting the ethical implications the specification asks for.
examTechnique.grade9Looks: A grade 9 answer names **all four** terms and explains **why sticky ends matter** — the same enzyme gives complementary overhangs, so the gene lands in the right place for ligase to seal. It separates the techniques by **mechanism**, noting that selective breeding can only use alleles the species **already has** while engineering can bring one from **another species**. It gives the named example, ***Bacillus thuringiensis***, and applies **natural selection** to predict that insects will evolve resistance to the toxin. It gives **reduced variation** as the risk shared by all three techniques, explains **eutrophication** as a chain, and — because the command is **evaluate** — supplies benefits, risks, an **ethical** implication, and a judgement that names what it depends on.
